subject: Unit-1 • Indus Valley Civilization and Major Sites
question: Which major archaeological site of the Harappan civilization is located on the left bank of the Ghaggar River in Hanumangarh district of Rajasthan, from where the oldest evidence of plowed fields and fire altars has been found?
verificationSource: Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) and R.S. Sharma (Ancient India)
explanation:
Kalibanga (black bangles), located on the banks of Ghagghar (ancient Saraswati) river in Hanumangarh district of Rajasthan, was discovered by Amlanand Ghosh in 1951 and B.B. Lal and B.K. Thapar got the excavation done. Here, evidence of transversely plowed fields has been found from the Pre-Harappan level, which indicates growing of two crops (gram and mustard) simultaneously. Apart from this, seven fire altars (Havan Kund) and ancient evidence of earthquake have also been found here.

subject: Unit-1 • Vedic Literature and Upanishads
question: The national motto 'Satyameva Jayate' inscribed in Devanagari script below the coat of arms of India is quoted from which of the following Upanishads?
verificationSource: Ancient Indian Literature and NCERT
explanation:
The national motto of India 'Satyameva Jayate' (Truth alone triumphs) is taken from the Mundaka Upanishad (Mundakopanishad, Mantra 3.1.6). In the same Upanishad, Yagya has been compared to a 'broken boat' (Adridha Hyete Yagyarupaah). Mandukya Upanishad is the shortest Upanishad in which the four Padas of Om are described, while in Kath Upanishad, the Yama-Nachiketa dialogue and in Chandogya, the first mention of Lord Krishna as the son of Devaki is found.

subject: Unit-1 • Maurya Empire and Officials
question:
Direction: Consider the following statements with reference to the inscriptions and administrative system of the Maurya emperor Ashoka.
1. Ashoka, in his 5th great inscription, has mentioned the appointment of new officials called 'Dhamma Mahamatra' for moral conduct and harmony in the society.
2. The 13th mega inscription gives a detailed description of the massacre of the Kalinga war, repentance and Dhamma-victory in the kingdoms of 5 Yavana kings.
3. In the Rummindei pillar inscription, there is mention of Ashoka completely waiving the religious tax 'sacrifice' of Lumbini, the birthplace of Buddha.
Which of the above statements are correct?
verificationSource: Inscriptions of Ashoka and Romila Thapar (Ashoka and the fall of the Maurya Empire)
explanation:
The above three statements (1, 2 and 3) are completely true historically. The 5th inscription of Ashoka describes the appointment of Dhamma Mahamatras in the 13th year of his coronation. The 13th inscription mentions the Kalinga war and Dhamma-victory in the kingdoms of five Yavana kings named Antioch, Turmaya, Antikini, Maga and Aliksundara. The Rummindei miniature pillar inscription located in the Terai of Nepal provides evidence of Ashoka's visit to Lumbini and reducing the religious tax 'Bali' to zero and reducing the land revenue 'Part' from 1/6 to 1/8.

[Chapter/Unit: Unit-1: History, Culture and National Movement of India. Subtopic: Maurya Empire and Officials. subject: Unit-1 • Sangam period and South Indian literature
question: Who was the author of the famous epic of Sangam literature, 'Silappadikaram' (Silappadikaram / Story of Nupur), which narrates the poignant story of Madurai merchant Kovalan, his wife Kannagi and dancer Madhavi?
verificationSource: K.A. Neelkanth Shastri (History of South India)
explanation:
'Shilappadikaram', the best of the five epics of Tamil literature, was composed by the Chera prince Ilango Adigal around 2nd-3rd century AD. In this, there is a description of the burning of Madurai city by his devoted wife Kannagi after the king of Pandya capital Madurai gave death sentence to innocent Kovalan and later the beginning of Kannagi (Pattini) puja. As its sequel, 'Manimekalai' was composed by Sittalai Sattanar, while Tolkappiyam is a Tamil grammar text.

question: Which scholar among the 'Navratnas' adorned in the Ujjain court of Gupta emperor Chandragupta II 'Vikramaditya' was the author of Sanskrit grammar and the famous Amarkosh (Sanskrit dictionary)?

subject: Unit-1 • Ancient University and Center of Education
question: The world famous 'Nalanda Mahavihara' (Nalanda University) located in Nalanda, Bihar was established by which Gupta emperor in the 5th century AD, where Hiuen Tsang studied?
verificationSource: History of Ancient India (KC Srivastava)
explanation:
Nalanda University was established in the 5th century by the Gupta ruler Kumaragupta I (415–455 AD, title: 'Mahendraditya'). According to the Chinese travelers Hiuen Tsang and Itsing, it received continuous patronage from the later Gupta, Harsha and Pala kings. Here Mahayana Buddhist philosophy was the main center and at that time Shilabhadra was its patriarch. In 1193 AD, Bakhtiyar Khilji had destroyed it by burning it.

subject: Unit-1 • Chola Architecture and Tanjore Temple
question: By which Chola emperor was the grand 'Brihadishvara Temple' (Rajarajeshvara Temple) with 13 storeys and 216 feet high vimana, symbolizing the culmination of Dravidian architecture, completed in 1010 AD in Thanjavur (Tanjore), Tamil Nadu?
verificationSource: Indian Art and Culture (Nitin Singhania) and NCERT
explanation:
The Brihadisvara Temple of Thanjavur (UNESCO World Heritage Site) was dedicated to Lord Shiva by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I (985–1014 AD). This is the world's first temple built entirely of granite stones. Its 13-storey pyramidal vimana is topped by an 80-tonne monolithic Kumbham (Shikhar Kalash) and has a huge monolithic statue of Nandi at its entrance. Rajendra I built a second Brihadisvara temple in his new capital Gangaikondacholapuram.

subject: Unit-1 • Delhi Sultanate (Ghulam Dynasty and Balban)
question: Which two Iranian/Persian etiquette traditions were made mandatory in the court by Sultan Ghiyasuddin Balban of Delhi Sultanate (1266–1287 AD) to establish the prestige of the Sultan?
options: Sijda (prostration to the ground) and Pabos (kissing the feet of the Sultan)
verificationSource: Tarikh-e-Firozshahi by Satish Chandra (Medieval India) and Barani
explanation:
Balban adopted Persian kingship traditions to establish the dignity and divine authority of the Sultan's office ('Niyabat-e-Khudai' and 'Zill-e-Ilahi' i.e. shadow of God). He made 'Sijda' (kneeling and bowing the head) and 'Pabos' (kissing the feet of the Sultan) mandatory in the court and started celebrating the Iranian New Year festival 'Nauroz'. He abolished Turk-e-Chahalgani (Chalisa Dal) and adopted the policy of 'Blood and Iron'.

subject: Unit-1 • Shershah Suri and Administrative Reforms
question: In medieval India, which ruler first issued 178 grain pure silver coin 'Rupiya' and 380 grain copper coin 'Dam', whose monetary system became the basis of modern Indian currency?
verificationSource: Tarikh-e-Shershahi by Abbas Khan Sarwani and NCERT
explanation:
Sher Shah Suri (1540–1545 AD), the founder of the Second Afghan (Sura) Empire, abolished the old distorted currencies and introduced a standard bi-metallic currency system. He introduced 'Rupee' worth 178 grains (silver) and 'Daam' worth 380 grains (copper). The exchange ratio of rupee and daum was 1:64. Akbar also adopted the same currency system of Sher Shah and this 'Rupee' remained the basic basis of Indian currency even during the British period.

subject: Unit-1 • Mughal Empire and Religious Policy (Ibadatkhana)
question: In which year did Mughal Emperor Akbar establish 'Ibadat Khana' (Prayer House) at Fatehpur Sikri to discuss religious and philosophical topics with scholars?
verificationSource: Abul Fazal (Akbarnama) and Badayuni (Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh)
explanation:
Akbar established 'Ibadat Khana' in his capital Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 AD. Initially it was only for Sunni Muslim scholars, but in 1578 AD, Akbar opened it for philosophers of all religions—Hindu (Purushottam and Devi), Jain (Harivijay Suri and Jinchandra Suri), Parsi (Dastur Meherji Rana) and Christian (Father Acquaviva and Monserrate). After this, 'Mahjar' (Infallible Declaration) was issued in 1579 and 'Tawheed-e-Ilahi' (Deen-e-Ilahi) was announced in 1582.

subject: Unit-1 • Land Revenue Settlement in British India
question: What was the ratio of the total land revenue collected between the British Company and the Zamindars respectively in the 'Permanent Settlement' (Istamari / Zamindari Settlement) implemented by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha in the year 1793?
verificationSource: B.L. Grover (History of Modern India)
explanation:
On 22 March 1793, under the plan of Governor-General Lord Cornwallis and John Shore, 'Permanent Settlement' came into force in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha and Banaras and North Karnataka (19% of the territory of British India). In this, the zamindars were considered as the permanent owners of the land and it was decided to deposit 10/11th part of the rent collected from them in the treasury of the East India Company and 1/11th part would be kept by the zamindar for his remuneration and expenses. 'Sunset Law' was implemented in 1794 for non-payment of taxes on time.

subject: Unit-1 • Indian National Congress and drain of wealth
question: In which historical book did India's 'Grand Old Man of India' Dadabhai Naoroji propound the economic theory of 'drain of wealth' from India to Britain due to British rule?
options: Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
verificationSource: Bipin Chandra (Rise of Economic Nationalism in Modern India)
explanation:
Dadabhai Naoroji first presented the theory of drain of wealth in the pamphlet 'England's Debt to India' read before the East India Association in London in 1867. In his immortal book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India', published from London in the year 1901, he proved that a large part of India's revenue is being sent to Britain in the form of 'Home Charges', salaries and pensions of officials and profits without any material return, due to which India is continuously becoming poor. Congress officially accepted it in the Calcutta session of 1896.

subject: Unit-2 • Geography of the World (Volcano and Magma Types)
question: With reference to the types of volcanoes, which of the following volcanic types is known as 'Caldera', which after its explosive eruption collapses into its own crater and forms a huge trough?
options: Shield volcanoes (such as Hawaiian Mauna Loa)
Caldera volcanoes (such as Krakatoa in Indonesia)
verificationSource: NCERT Fundamentals of Physical Geography (Chapter: Landforms)
explanation:
The most explosive volcanoes on Earth are called 'Caldera'. Their eruption is so intense and explosive that when the magma chamber is empty, its top cone sinks inwards instead of forming a mountain of lava outside, creating a huge bowl-shaped trough (caldera) several kilometers wide in which the caldera lake is later formed. Indonesia's Krakatoa and Taupo are prime examples. Shield volcanoes (Hawaiian Islands) are formed from low viscosity liquid basalt and have low slopes.

subject: Unit-2 • Geography of the World (Karst Landforms)
question: What are the concrete-like pillars hanging down from the ceiling of caves due to chemical deposition of underground water in areas of limestone (Karst) called?
verificationSource: Savandra Singh (Physical Geography) and NCERT
explanation:
In karst caves, when calcium bicarbonate dissolved in water seeping from the ceiling evaporates, sharp columns of lime hanging from the ceiling are called 'stalactites'. The flat pillars formed from bottom to top by water dripping on the floor are called 'Stalagmite'. When both join together, it is called 'Cave Pillar'. Lapis and dolines are erosional landforms created by water.

subject: Unit-2 • Plants and trees of Uttarakhand (Oak tree) (Uttarakhand special)
question: Which broad-leafed temperate evergreen tree is found in the central Himalayan region of Uttarakhand (1200 to 2400 meters), which is called 'boon of mountains' and 'green gold' due to its high water-holding capacity and soil conservation properties?
verificationSource: Uttarakhand Forest Research Division and Environmental Studies
explanation:
The oak tree of the oak family (botanical name: Quercus leucotrichophora) is the lifeline of the central Himalayas of Uttarakhand. Its deep roots and the rotten manure of leaves absorb rainwater like a sponge and recharge the ground water due to which natural water sources (rivers and streams) remain alive for twelve months. Its leaves provide the best fodder and wood provides excellent fuel for cattle. In the Chipko movement, women gave the slogan – 'What are the benefits of the forest? subject: Unit-3 • Constitutional Development and Charter Act of 1833
question: By which Charter Act during the British rule, the designation of 'Governor-General of Bengal' was changed to 'Governor-General of India' and all civil and military powers were vested in him, making Lord William Bentinck the first Governor-General of India?
verificationSource: Constitutional History (M. Laxmikant and D.D. Basu)
explanation:
The Charter Act of 1833 took a decisive step towards centralization of administration in India. By this, the Governor-General of Bengal was made the 'Governor-General of India' and legislative powers were taken away from the Governors of Bombay and Madras. Lord William Bentinck became the first Governor-General of India. This Act completely ended all commercial functions of the East India Company, including its tea and trade monopoly with China, making it a purely administrative body, and the first Law Commission was constituted under the chairmanship of Lord Macaulay.

subject: Unit-3 • Preamble of the Constitution
question:
Direction: Consider the following statements in the context of 'Right to Education' in the Indian Constitution and the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002.
1. By this amendment, by adding a new Article 21A in Part-III of the Constitution, elementary education was made a fundamental right for children of 6 to 14 years.
2. By this amendment, the 11th fundamental duty (to provide opportunities for education to children by parents) was added to Article 51A.
3. To implement this right, the 'Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act' was immediately implemented by the Parliament in the year 2002 itself.
Which of the above statements are correct?
verificationSource: Constitution of India and 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976
explanation:
Statements 1 and 2 are correct, but statement 3 is incorrect. The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 made education a fundamental right under Article 21A and added the 11th fundamental duty under Article 51A(k). Statement 3 is incorrect because the Act of Parliament 'Right to Education Act' (RTE Act) implementing this constitutional right was passed in the year 2009 and came into effect across the country from 1 April 2010, and not in 2002.

[Chapter/Unit: Unit-3: Indian Polity and Constitution | Subtopic: Preamble of the Constitution. Question Type: Statement-based MCQ | Difficulty Level: Easy | Uttarakhand-linked: No | Verification source: Constitution of India and 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976]

subject: Unit-3 • Fundamental Rights (Right to Education Article 21A)
question: By which historic Constitutional Amendment Act 'Article 21A' was added to the Constitution making elementary education a fundamental right for all children in the age group of 6 to 14 years?
verificationSource: Constitution of India (Article 21A and 86th Constitutional Amendment)
explanation:
During the tenure of the Atal Bihari Vajpayee government, a three-tier legal basis was given to education by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002: (1) Free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years was made a 'fundamental right' by adding Article 21A in Part-III; (2) By amending Article 45, instructions for care and education of children below 6 years of age were given in the Directive Principles of Policy; And (3) The 11th fundamental duty (51A(k)) was added to Article 51A that parents should provide opportunities for education to their children. To implement this, 'Right to Education Act, 2009' came into effect from 1 April 2010.

subject: Unit-3 • Directive Principles of State Policy (Gandhian and Liberal Principles)
question: Which of the following articles included in the Directive Principles of Policy (DPSP) of the Indian Constitution is not purely based on 'Gandhian Principles'?

Article 48A (Protection, promotion and protection of environment and wildlife)
Article 47 (Prohibition of consumption of alcoholic beverages and harmful intoxicants)
verificationSource: Constitution of India (Part-IV) and Grenville Austin
explanation:
The Directive Principles of Policy are divided into three ideological categories—socialist, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual. Article 40 (Gram Panchayats), Article 43 (Cottage Industries), Article 43B (Cooperative Societies), Article 46 (Educational-economic interests of weaker sections/SC-ST), Article 47 (Prohibition/Health) and Article 48 (Ban on slaughter of milch animals and cattle) are based on Gandhian principles. subject: Unit-3 • India's Foreign Policy (Gujral Doctrine)
question: In 1996, the then Foreign Minister (and later Prime Minister) I.K. What is the historical principle of India's foreign policy propounded by Gujral called, under which India resolved to give unilateral concessions to its small neighboring countries without any reciprocity?

subject: Unit-4 • Macroeconomics and Phillips Curve
question:
Direction: Consider the following statements in the context of 'Phillips Curve' and inflation in macroeconomics.
1. The traditional short-run Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship between the inflation rate and the unemployment rate.
2. According to economist Milton Friedman, in the long run the Phillips curve becomes vertical at the natural unemployment rate (NAIRU).
3. In the case of 'Stagflation', along with high inflation, the unemployment rate also reaches extremely high levels, due to which the short-term Phillips curve gets disintegrated.
Which of the above statements are correct?
verificationSource: Macro Economics (NCERT Class 12 & H.L. Ahuja)
explanation:
The above three statements (1, 2 and 3) are completely correct according to economic principles. In 1958 A.W. Phillips presented a trade-off between inflation and unemployment in the short run. In the 1970s, Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps proved that the Phillips curve becomes vertical at the natural unemployment rate (NAIRU) when adjusted for long-run inflation expectations. When the oil crisis of the 1970s led to stagflation (high inflation + high unemployment + economic recession), the traditional Phillips curve failed.

[Chapter/Unit: Unit-4: Economic and Social Development | Subtopic: Macroeconomics and Phillips Curve. Question Type: Statement-based MCQ | Difficulty Level: Moderate | Uttarakhand-linked: No | Verification Source: Macroeconomics (NCERT Class 12 & H.L. Ahuja)]

subject: Unit-4 • Banking Regulation and Basel Norms

explanation:
The Basel Committee on Bank Supervision (BCBS), based in Basel, Switzerland, has created capital adequacy rules to protect banks from bankruptcy. Additionally, after adding 'Capital Conservation Buffer' (CCB) of 2.5%, the total regulatory capital level of banks is required to be minimum 11.5%.

subject: Unit-4 • Financial Inclusion and Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana
question:
Given below are two statements, one of which is labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Very high 'Fiscal Deficit' in the economy often causes the 'Current Account Deficit' of the country to increase.
Reason (R): Heavy borrowing by the government to finance high fiscal deficit increases domestic consumption demand, which increases imports and reduces national savings.
Select the correct answer from the codes given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
verificationSource: Department of Financial Services (DFS, Union Finance Ministry)
explanation:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A). This is called 'Twin Deficit Hypothesis' in macroeconomics. According to the national income equation (S – I) + (T – G) = (X – M), if the government budget deficit (G – T) increases and private savings do not increase as much, the country needs external financing. This artificial increase in domestic demand increases imports, thereby increasing the trade deficit and current account deficit (CAD).

subject: Unit-4 • Fiscal Policy and Twin Deficit
question: When 'High Fiscal Deficit' and 'High Current Account Deficit' (CAD) exist together in an economy, then what is this macroeconomic situation known as?
verificationSource: Economic Survey (Union Finance Ministry) and Macroeconomics
explanation:
In the economy, when both the government's budget deficit/fiscal deficit (government expenditure being more than revenue) and the country's external current account deficit (import of goods and services being more than export) both increase excessively, then it is called 'Twin Deficit'. Higher fiscal deficit increases domestic demand which boosts imports and lower national saving leads to higher current account deficit, which risks devaluation of the domestic currency and pressure on foreign exchange reserves.

maximum at the equator and minimum at the poles
Maximum at the poles and minimum at the equator.
completely uniform everywhere on the earth's surface
verificationSource: NCERT Class 9 & 11 Physics (Gravitation)
explanation:
The formula for gravitational acceleration is g = GM / R², where R is the radius of the Earth. subject: Unit-5 • Chemistry (Greenhouse Gases and Global Warming Potential)
question:
Instructions: DNA Consider the following statements with reference to the structure and genetic organization of DNA.
1. In the year 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick discovered DNA. Proposed the double helix model.
2. DNA There are two hydrogen bonds between adenine (A) and thymine (T) and three hydrogen bonds between guanine (G) and cytosine (C).
3. According to Chargaff's rules, D.N.A. The ratio of purine bases (A + G) in the double strand is always equal to that of pyrimidine bases (T + C).
Which of the above statements are correct?
verificationSource: IPCC Climate Change Assessment Report and NCERT
explanation:
The above three statements (1, 2 and 3) are the fundamental truths of molecular biology. In 1953, Watson and Crick gave a DNA double helix model based on X-ray diffraction data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins. In this, A = T (two hydrogen bonds) and G ≡ C (three hydrogen bonds) are found in complementary base pairing. According to Erwin Chargaff's rule, in any double-stranded DNA [A] = [T] and [G] = [C], hence the total ratio of purine and pyrimidine bases is always 1:1.

verificationSource: NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (Nuclear Chemistry) and Archeology
explanation:
Radiocarbon dating was discovered in the 1940s by the American chemist Willard Libby (for which he received the Nobel Prize in 1960). Carbon-14 (¹⁴C), formed from nitrogen-14 by cosmic rays in the atmosphere, enters all living organisms in stable proportions through photosynthesis and food. After the death of the organism, new absorption of ¹⁴C stops and it begins to decay with a half-life of 5,730 years. subject: Unit-5 • Environmental Pollution and Biomagnification
question: What is the continuous increase in the concentrations of non-biodegradable pollutants (such as DDT and heavy metal mercury) at successive trophic levels as they pass through different trophic levels of a food chain called in ecology?
verificationSource: Environmental Biology and NCERT Class 12
explanation:
When fat-soluble non-biodegradable chemicals like DDT, PCBs or methyl mercury enter the food chain, organisms are unable to metabolize or excrete them. Accumulation of a toxic substance during the lifetime of an organism is called 'bioaccumulation', whereas the increase in its concentration thousands-millions of times in each successive trophic level from the lower trophic level (phytoplankton) to the top consumer (fish-eating bird or human) in the food chain is called 'biomagnification'. For example, DDT causes the shells of pelican and eagle eggs to become thin.

subject: Unit-5 • Water Pollution and Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD)
question: What does an increase in the value of 'Biological Oxygen Demand' (BOD) mean, used to assess the level of pollution in a water body (river or lake)?
options: Presence of heavy metals in water is zero
The water is very pure and drinkable
There is more organic pollution in water and the level of dissolved oxygen (DO) in water is decreasing.
water temperature is getting very low
verificationSource: Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and water quality standards
explanation:
Biological oxygen demand (BOD) is the amount of oxygen (mg/L) consumed by microorganisms (bacteria) to decompose organic matter present in 1 liter of water in 5 days at 20°C. If there is more sewage, sewage or industrial organic waste in the water, the bacteria will grow faster and require more oxygen, which will increase the BOD value and 'Dissolved Oxygen' (DO) in the water will fall dangerously for aquatic organisms. The BOD of pure drinking water is less than 1 mg/L, while that of polluted sewage reaches 100-400 mg/L.

explanation:

Religiously it is especially offered to Lord Shiva and Vishnu in Kedarnath and Badrinath Dham.

subject: Unit-5 • Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) in Uttarakhand (Uttarakhand Special)
question: What is called in scientific terminology the devastating floods caused by the sudden rupture of moraine-obstructed lakes formed by the melting of glaciers in the high Himalayan regions due to climate change?
options: Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF - Glacial Lake Outburst Flood)
verificationSource: Uttarakhand State Disaster Management Authority (USDMA) and Wadia Institute
explanation:
A 'glacial lake outburst flood' (GLOF) occurs when a naturally unstable lake formed by the accumulation of ice and loose debris (moraine) behind a glacier suddenly bursts due to extreme water pressure, avalanche or earthquake. As a result, millions of liters of water and boulders flood the lower river basin at a rapid speed and cause devastation (like the breach of Chorabari pond in Kedarnath in 2013). Uttarakhand State Disaster Management Authority (USDMA) and ISRO are currently continuously monitoring 13 hyper-sensitive glacial lakes of the state through satellite.
